For investors assessing Intel’s foundry ambitions, Naga Chandrasekaran is a central figure. As Intel Foundry’s chief technology and operations officer and general manager, he oversees the work of turning manufacturing plans into processes that customers can use at scale. His responsibilities span technology development, factory execution and foundry services.

The questions for an investor tour are practical. Can Intel ramp its advanced manufacturing processes reliably? Can it deliver competitive yields and costs? And can it persuade outside chip designers to commit products to its factories? Announcements about process technology matter, but customer commitments and consistent production will provide stronger evidence of progress.

Chandrasekaran’s perspective matters because a foundry must do more than demonstrate a promising chip. It must reproduce that result across large volumes while meeting customers’ schedules, performance targets and quality requirements. Intel has also emphasized advanced packaging as part of its foundry offering, adding another measure of execution.

For investors, the distinction is between a credible roadmap and a profitable business built on it. Intel’s progress will be judged by manufacturing milestones, external customer adoption and financial results over time. I could not verify a specific KeyBanc tour with Chandrasekaran from the public material available, so these are the issues such a discussion would raise, not a report of remarks he made there.
